paragraphs: Tzarik lesheb baavir sukka, vehayyashen tachat hammitta im yesh miggag hammitta ad laaretz asara tepachim lo yatza yede chobato, vetzarik lizzaher shello yashen tachat shulchan sheggabohha asara tepachim:

clarification.explanation: The mitzvah of sukkah requires actually sitting and sleeping directly under the open air of the sekhach (covering). Therefore, one who sleeps under a bed, where there are ten handbreadths from the top of the bed to the floor, has the bed itself become a tent (ohel) that separates between him and the sekhach, and he has not fulfilled the mitzvah of sukkah. Likewise, one must be careful not to sleep under a table that is ten handbreadths high or more, for the same reason.
takeaways: One may not sleep under a bed or table that is ten handbreadths high, since it becomes a tent separating from the sekhach
One must ensure he is directly exposed to the open air of the sekhach while sleeping

paragraphs: Yizzaher laasot haddepanot qodem hassekak veim lehepek pesula, veyizzaher shello yannicha dabar hamqabbel tuma bassekak, velaken haetzim shel hassekak lo yihyeh bahem bet qibbul deaz meqabbelim tuma, umechamat ken yizzaher gam ken shello yannicha etzim shel hammitta bassekak mippene shehem meqabbelim tuma, vehapperot hem meqabbelim tuma velaken lo yitleh rimmonim vekayyotze bassekak, ella raq bepachot mearbaa tepachim benehem leben hassekak, deaz ap al pi shehem meqabbelim tuma kevan dehu toleh otam lenoy bateli legabbe sekak vela mippesil mishshum sekak pasul abal im yesh arbaa tepachim la bateli legabbe sekak vehave perot ellu sekak pasul, veap al gab deen rechabim arbaa tepachim gazerinan attu rechabim arbaa, mihu bimnora deikka chashash deleqa im yitlenna bepachot min arbaa tepachim muttar litlotah shiur arbaa tepachim o yoter dachashib zeh kediabad, ak yizzaher shello yashen tachteha:

clarification.explanation: One must build the walls of the sukkah before the sekhach; if he did the reverse (placed the sekhach before there were walls), the sukkah is invalid. One must be careful not to place in the sekhach anything susceptible to tumah — therefore the wood of the sekhach should not be of a type that has a 'beit kibbul' (a receptacle able to hold things), because such articles are susceptible to tumah. For the same reason one must be careful not to use bed-wood as sekhach, since it is liable to become susceptible to tumah. Fruits, too, are susceptible to tumah, so one should not hang pomegranates and the like directly within the sekhach itself — only if they are hung within four handbreadths of the sekhach (right next to it) are they considered nullified in relation to the sekhach and not disqualifying, since they are only for decoration. But if they are four handbreadths away or more, they themselves are considered part of the sekhach and invalidate it (and even if they are not four handbreadths wide, the Sages decreed against this on account of ones that are four handbreadths wide). Regarding a lamp where there is concern of fire, if there is no choice, it is permitted to hang it even at a distance of four handbreadths or more from the sekhach, but one must be careful not to sleep beneath it (for the reason stated in the previous halacha — not to sleep under something that blocks at a height of ten handbreadths).
takeaways: The walls must be built first, and only afterward the sekhach
Bed-wood may not be used as sekhach; decorative hanging fruit is valid only within four handbreadths of the sekhach
A hanging lamp is permitted for safety reasons even at a distance, but one must not sleep beneath it

paragraphs: Lo yokal beereb sukkot mechatzot veelak, kede sheyyokal ballayla leteabon ki haakila ballayla harishona deorayeta vekaasher nebaer beezrat hashshem, veha desaggi beereb pesach mishshaa asirit vekan tzarik lehizzaher mechatzot, haynu ki belel pesach okelim hammatztza achar qeriat hahaggada sheshshohin zeman harbeh veim yizzaher mishshaa asirit yesh zeman harbeh ad sheyyaggia akilat matztza, mah sheen ken besukkot hu okel miyyad keshettechshak lekak tzarik lehizzaher limnoa haakila mechatzot vekannizkar baacharonim:

clarification.explanation: On the eve of Sukkot one should not eat a fixed meal from midday onward, so that the person will reach the eating of the first night (which is a Torah obligation) hungry and eager to eat. The Ben Ish Chai explains why here one must be careful specifically from midday, whereas on the eve of Passover it suffices to refrain from eating starting from the tenth hour of the day: at the Seder, the matzah is eaten only after the reading of the Haggadah, which takes a long time, so even if one begins refraining from eating only at the tenth hour, there is still a long time until the eating of the matzah for the appetite to return. On the night of Sukkot, by contrast, one eats immediately when night falls, without a long interval, and therefore one must be careful to refrain from eating already from midday of that day.
takeaways: One should not eat a meal on the eve of Sukkot from midday onward
The purpose is to arrive at the first night's meal in the sukkah with appetite, since it is a Torah obligation

paragraphs: Yeqaddesh achar sheyyihyeh layla vadday, ubelel rishon yebarek "lesheb bassukka" veachar kak "shehecheyanu", ki birkat "shehecheyanu" qae al hassukka veal qiddush yom tob, abal belel sheni yebarek "shehecheyanu" veachar kak "lesheb bassukka":

clarification.explanation: Kiddush on the night of Sukkot should be recited only after it is certainly night (not during bein hashmashot, twilight). On the first night one blesses 'Leishev BaSukkah' and only afterward 'Shehecheyanu,' because on that night the blessing of Shehecheyanu applies both to the mitzvah of the sukkah and to the Kiddush of the festival together. But on the second night one blesses 'Shehecheyanu' first and only afterward 'Leishev BaSukkah' (the reverse order).
takeaways: First night: 'Leishev BaSukkah' then 'Shehecheyanu'
Second night: 'Shehecheyanu' then 'Leishev BaSukkah'

paragraphs: Bekol et sheyyesh qadosh yebarek "lesheb bassukka" achar birkat qiddush ubeet shello yesh qiddush yesh nohagin lebarek "lesheb bassukka" qodem birkat "hammotzi" achar birkat "al netilat yadayim"; veyesh nohagin lebarek "lesheb bassukka" achar birkat "hammotzi" qodem sheyyokal veen chashub hepseq dehave k"gebil letore", vaanachnu bebetenu mizzeman ateret roshenu harab haggaon mv"r zeqeni rabbenu mosheh chayyim za"l minhagenu lebarek "lesheb bassukka" qodem birkat "hammotzi" veken iqqar, ubekol paam shemmebarek "lesheb bassukka" yebarek meummad veachar kak yesheb vekannizkar baacharonim. veim shakach velo berek qodem akila yebarek kol zeman shello siyyem akilato, veim hu mesuppaq im berak o lav lo yebarek veim yirtzeh lebarek birkat hammazon kede sheyyittol yadayv vibarek "lesheb bassukka" veyokal hareshut beyado, veen bazeh chashash gorem beraka sheenah tzerika:

clarification.explanation: Whenever there is a Kiddush (such as on nights and days when there is an obligation of Kiddush), one blesses 'Leishev BaSukkah' immediately after the blessing of Kiddush. At times when there is no Kiddush, some have the custom to bless 'Leishev BaSukkah' after the blessing of 'Al Netilat Yadayim' and before the blessing of 'HaMotzi'; and some have the custom to bless 'Leishev BaSukkah' after the blessing of 'HaMotzi' and before the eating itself — and this is not considered an invalid interruption (comparable to 'gevil le-torei' — an incidental act permitted as a direct continuation of the main action). In the family of the Ben Ish Chai (since the time of his grandfather, Rabbi Moshe Chaim), the fixed custom was to bless 'Leishev BaSukkah' before the blessing of 'HaMotzi,' and this is the primary halachic practice. Every time one blesses 'Leishev BaSukkah,' one should bless standing and then sit. One who forgot to bless before eating may bless at any time before he finishes his meal. If he is uncertain whether he already blessed or not, he should not bless again (following the principle of being lenient in cases of doubt regarding blessings); but if he wishes to recite Birkat HaMazon in any case, he may wash his hands anew, bless 'Leishev BaSukkah,' and eat a little more — and he may do so without concern of making 'a blessing that is not necessary.'
takeaways: The primary custom (of the Ben Ish Chai's family) is to bless 'Leishev BaSukkah' before the blessing of HaMotzi
The blessing of 'Leishev BaSukkah' is always recited standing
If in doubt whether one already blessed, one does not bless again, but may remedy this by washing anew and eating again

paragraphs: Belel rishon ubelel sheni ledidan deyatebi bechutz laaretz tzarik lekavven baakilato bikzayit rishon shehu chiyyub deorayeta kemo kezayit matztza belel pesach, vetob sheyyeparesh dabar zeh bepiv kesheomer "leshem yichud qadesha berik hu ushekinatah" qodem akila, vetzarik leekol yoter mikkabbetza pat lekulle alema:

clarification.explanation: On the first night (and, for those outside the Land of Israel, also on the second night) of Sukkot, one must have intent while eating the first olive-sized portion of bread that this is a Torah obligation, exactly like the kezayit of matzah on the night of the Seder. It is good to state this intention explicitly in speech when reciting the formula 'Leshem Yichud Kudsha Berich Hu U'Shechinteih' before eating. One must eat, in that same eating, more than the measure of an egg's worth of bread, according to all opinions.
takeaways: On the first night (and, for those outside the Land, also the second night) there is a Torah obligation to eat a kezayit of bread in the sukkah with special intent
One must eat more than an egg's worth of bread to fulfill the obligation according to all opinions

paragraphs: Bekol layla qodem sheyyikkanes lassukka yomar "leshem yichud qadesha berik hu ushekinatah veku' kemo shetztzivvanu Adonai elohenu al yede mosheh rabbenu alayv hashshalom "bassukkot teshebu shibat yamim kol haezrach beyisrael yeshebu bassukkot lemaan yedeu dorotekem ki bassukkot hoshabti et bene yisrael behotzii otam meeretz mitzrayim" (vayyiqra kg, mb), sheggam lepi daat happoseqim happashtanim yesh chiyyub leparesh pasuq zeh kullo bepiv bemitzva zo, veyizzaher lilmod mishna masseket sukka bekol layla bekol yemot hechag betok hassukka, vehammabdil bebeto yabdil bassukka:

clarification.explanation: Every night of the festival, before entering the sukkah, one should recite the formula 'Leshem Yichud Kudsha Berich Hu U'Shechinteih,' and continue by stating that the mitzvah is being fulfilled as God commanded through Moshe Rabbeinu — reciting the entire verse 'In sukkot shall you dwell seven days; every citizen in Israel shall dwell in sukkot, so that your generations will know that I caused the Children of Israel to dwell in sukkot when I brought them out of the land of Egypt.' For even according to the authorities who interpret matters in the plain sense (not only by way of the esoteric/kabbalistic tradition), there is an obligation to recite this entire verse aloud as part of this mitzvah. One should also take care to study a Mishnah from Tractate Sukkah every night of the festival, within the sukkah itself. One who performs Havdalah [at the end of Shabbat] should perform it inside the sukkah.
takeaways: Before entering the sukkah each night, one should recite the verse 'In sukkot shall you dwell' in full
One should study a Mishnah from Tractate Sukkah every night, inside the sukkah
Havdalah on a Shabbat that falls during the festival is performed inside the sukkah

paragraphs: Lo yebarek lesheb bassukka ella bepat gamur, abal bepat habbaa bekisnin shebbirkato "mezonot" lo yebarek mishshum sapeq berakot lehaqel, ubekol et sheyyebarek "lesheb bassukka" yekavven liptor bibraka zo yeshibato vaakilato veshinto ad zeman akilat pat hashshenit achar zo, veap al pi demin haddin muttar leekol akilat aray chutz lassukka, im kol zeh hammachmir shello lishtot apillu mayim chutz lassukka tabo alayv beraka, abal shena apillu shinat aray asur lishon chutz lassukka, lepikak im roeh adam chabero bebet hakkeneset mitnamnem beet qeriat seper tora vekayyotze tzarik leorer oto:

clarification.explanation: One blesses 'Leishev BaSukkah' only when eating full-fledged bread (lechem); but over 'pat haba'ah bekisnin' (pastries whose blessing is 'Mezonot' rather than 'HaMotzi'), one does not bless 'Leishev BaSukkah,' due to the principle of being lenient in cases of doubt regarding blessings. Every time one blesses 'Leishev BaSukkah,' he should intend, through this one blessing, to cover his sitting in the sukkah, his eating, and his sleeping — until the time he eats bread again. Although strictly by the letter of the law it is permitted to eat a casual meal outside the sukkah, one who is stringent with himself and does not even drink water outside the sukkah is worthy of blessing. Sleep, by contrast — even a casual nap — is entirely forbidden outside the sukkah; therefore, one who sees his fellow dozing in the synagogue during the Torah reading or the like must wake him (so that he not sleep outside the sukkah).
takeaways: 'Leishev BaSukkah' is blessed only over full-fledged bread, not over Mezonot foods
Sleep is entirely forbidden outside the sukkah, even a casual nap — so one must wake those who doze off

paragraphs: Bekol layla yishlach qeara tabshil leezeh ani, vehu cheleq shiba ushpizin qaddishin, vehassukka hi tzila demehemanuta zeker leanne kabod laken lo yinhog bah sechoq veqallut rosh, gam lo yaknis qederot uqearot gedolot shel tabshil sheddarkam lehannicham bebet hattabshil, veken lo yannicha bah kad haggadol shel hammayim, vehanner achar shekkaba yesirennu min hassukka velo yishshaer sham achar shekkaba vekannizkar ballebush, gam lo yirchatz betok hassukka kelim vaapillu keli echad bilbad vekannizkar baacharonim, mihu keli qatan beyoter sheshshotin bo qhvv" (qapeh) im hu lebaddo- let lan bah, veabit me raglayim lo yaknis lassukka ap al pi sheddarko bishar yemot hashshana lehakniso becheder shehu yashen bo, mihu tashmish hammitta muttar besukka:

clarification.explanation: Every night of the festival it is proper to send a bowl of cooked food to some poor person, as part of the concept of the 'seven holy guests' (Ushpizin Kadishin) who visit the sukkah. The sukkah is considered 'tzila demeheimanuta' (the shade of faith) — commemorating the Clouds of Glory that accompanied Israel in the wilderness — and therefore one should not behave in it with levity or frivolity. One should not bring into it large cooking pots and bowls (of the kind normally kept in the kitchen), nor a large water jug. A lamp that has gone out should be removed from the sukkah rather than left there. One should not wash dishes inside the sukkah, even a single dish — except for a very small vessel used for drinking coffee, which is permitted if it is alone. A chamber pot should not be brought into the sukkah at all, even though during the rest of the year it is customarily kept in the bedroom. Nevertheless, marital relations themselves are permitted in the sukkah.
takeaways: One must treat the sukkah with great respect and not bring large kitchen vessels or a chamber pot into it
It is proper to send a portion of food to a poor person every night of the festival

paragraphs: Asur lehanot min haokalin shettolin bassukka lenoy bekol yom tob kullo dehuqtzu, umuttarin belel isru chag im lo chal beshabbat, veim napelu beyom tob muqtzin hem veasur letaltelam ella yabiu qatan ben shelosh o arba shanim vitaltelem lemaqom acher lehatzniam sham ad achar yom tob; vaapillu qesam lachtzotz shinnayv asur liqqach min hassukka vaapillu min haddepanot, mihu im yeredu geshamim yasir hassedinin shettolin baddepanot davqa kede shello yitqalqelu, lepikak keshettoleh hassedinin baddepanot qodem yom tob yizzaher shello yittalem al yede qesharim, deim ken im yeredu geshamim beyom tob asur lehattir qesharim shel qayma, ella yetallem beopen shello yitztarek lehattir qesharim:

clarification.explanation: It is forbidden to derive benefit from fruits or foods hung in the sukkah for decoration, throughout all the days of the festival, since they have been 'set aside' (dedicated for decoration and not for eating). One may benefit from them only on the night of Isru Chag, provided that night does not fall on Shabbat. If such a decorative fruit falls from the sukkah on Yom Tov, it remains muktzeh and it is forbidden to move it; the solution is to bring a small child aged three to four (who is not bound by the laws of muktzeh) to move it to another place until after the festival. Even a toothpick may not be taken from the sukkah, not even from the walls. If rain falls, one is permitted to remove the sheets hung as walls so that they not be ruined — therefore, when hanging sheets before the festival, one must be careful to hang them in a way that will not require untying knots (since, if they are tied with permanent knots, it is forbidden to untie them on Yom Tov).
takeaways: It is forbidden to benefit from decorative food items in the sukkah throughout the festival (muktzeh)
If such a decoration falls, it may only be moved by a young child
When hanging sheets as walls, avoid knots that cannot be untied, so they can be removed if it rains

paragraphs: Qatan hecharip mittechillat chamesh shanim chayyab abiv lechanneko bemitzvat sukka, veeno charip mittechillat shesh shanim, veyesh omerim: hecharip ad sheyyigmor hechamesh shanim, veeno charip ad sheyyigmor shesh, vehannashim ap al pi demin haddin peturim mishshum desukka mitzvat aseh shehazzeman geramah, im kol zeh im yeshebu bassukka yesh lahem sekar mitzva:

clarification.explanation: A young child who is 'chariff' (sharp-minded, understanding) already from the age of five, his father is obligated to educate him in the mitzvah of sukkah; if he is not sharp-minded, the education begins only from age six. Some say that the age for chinuch depends specifically on the completion of the year (not its beginning): according to this view, the sharp child becomes obligated only after he has completed five full years (later than the first opinion, which begins already at the start of the fifth year), and one who is not sharp-minded — only after he has completed six full years. Women are exempt from the mitzvah of sukkah by strict law, since it is a positive time-bound commandment, but if they nevertheless sit in the sukkah, they receive reward for it as for the fulfillment of a mitzvah.
takeaways: Education in the mitzvah of sukkah: a sharp child from age five, a non-sharp child from age six
Women are exempt from sukkah but receive reward if they sit in it anyway

paragraphs: Choleh apillu chash berosho o chash beenayv patur im yesh lo menucha chutz lassukka, veim en hepresh chayyab, abal layla rishona apillu choleh chayyab leekol kazzayit bassukka, vehammitztaer mippene harecha o yattushin vekayyotze patur min hassukka, mihu tzarik sheyyihyeh lo tzaar shiur shedderek bene adam lehitztaer bo, abal im hu mepunnaq umitztaer al dabar muat eno patur, vekol zeh davqa im yatza min hassukka yinnatzel mitztzaar zeh, abal im ap al pi sheyyatza yaggia lo zeh hatztzaar shel recha o yattushin vekayyotze eno yakol liptor atzmo min hassukka, vesukka sheyyeshenim bah bene adam harbeh veeno yakol lishon bepashut yadayim veraglayim, la chashib zeh tzaar liptor atzmo bekak velatzet missukka:

clarification.explanation: A sick person, even one who merely has a headache or eye pain, is exempt from the mitzvah of sukkah if he has better rest outside the sukkah; but if there is no difference between being in the sukkah or outside it, he is obligated. Nevertheless, on the first night, even a sick person is obligated to eat a kezayit of bread in the sukkah (due to that night's special Torah obligation). One who suffers in the sukkah from a bad odor or from mosquitoes and the like is exempt from it, but only if this is a degree of distress that most people would be bothered by; one who is especially sensitive ('delicate') and is distressed by a minor matter is not exempt. All of this applies specifically when leaving the sukkah will actually solve the problem; but if the same odor or mosquitoes will reach him even outside the sukkah, he has no exemption and must remain in the sukkah. A crowded sukkah in which many people sleep, such that one cannot sleep with arms and legs outstretched, is not considered sufficient distress to exempt oneself and leave the sukkah.
takeaways: A sick person is exempt from the sukkah only if there is a real difference in his rest inside versus outside; on the first night he is nevertheless obligated in the kezayit
Distress from odor or mosquitoes exempts one only if leaving actually resolves it, and only if it is ordinary distress rather than excessive sensitivity
Ordinary crowding in the sukkah is not considered distress that exempts one from the mitzvah

paragraphs: Yebarek "al netilat lulab" v"shehecheyanu" qodem sheyyittol haetrog, abal hallulab yittelennu beyado qodem sheyyebarek, veim karuk beged al yado mishshum chabbura yesirennu qodem habberaka musham chatzitza, veyesh omerim sheyyasir gam hattabbaat meetzbao, veim shakach velo hesir yittol shenit belo beraka, veyizzaher sheyyasim hashshidra shel hallulab keneged panayv beet habberaka vehanninua, veasur leekol qodem sheyyebarek al hallulab:

clarification.explanation: One blesses 'Al Netilat Lulav' and 'Shehecheyanu' even before taking the etrog, but the lulav itself must be held in the hand before reciting the blessing. If there is a cloth wrapped around the hand (to prevent injury from the spikes), one should remove it before the blessing, since it is considered an interposition; and some say one should also remove a ring from the finger. One who forgot and did not remove it should take the lulav again without repeating the blessing. One must be careful to hold the spine (the hard back) of the lulav facing toward his face at the time of the blessing and the waving. It is forbidden to eat before blessing on the taking of the lulav.
takeaways: Any interposition (cloth, ring) must be removed from the hand before the lulav blessing
During the blessing, the spine of the lulav should face toward one's face
It is forbidden to eat before taking the lulav and reciting its blessing

paragraphs: Apillu choleh yebarek veyittol lulab meummad, vetzarik sheyyittol hallulab beyamin vehaetrog bismol, veyizzaher bekak gam bahaqqapot keshemmaqqip ballulab, ki yesh toin bazeh sheochazim hallulab vehaetrog beyad achat vehassiddur sheqqorin bo hahoshana bayyad hashshenit, vezeh eno nakon ella gam bahaqqapot yochaz haetrog bismol velulab beyamin, veyizzaher shello yaprid haetrog min hallulab bishat beraka sheppogem bekak, vetzarik lechabber haetrog im hallulab besopo ukemo shekkatab rabbenu za"l beseper hakkavvanot vezeh leshono: laken meqom chibbur haheetrug al yad hallulab hu besiyyuma, bimqom achizato millematta ki ken haatara hi besop hayyesod; ad kan leshono; ayyen sham; velaken tzarik lehizzaher bazeh:

clarification.explanation: Even a sick person blesses and takes the lulav while standing. One must hold the lulav in the right hand and the etrog in the left hand — and one must be careful about this also during the hakafot (the circling of the bimah with the lulav on Sukkot). Some mistakenly hold the lulav and etrog together in one hand and the prayer book (from which the Hoshanot text is read) in the other hand — this is incorrect; even during the hakafot one should hold the etrog in the left hand and the lulav in the right. One must be careful not to separate the etrog from the lulav at the time of the blessing, since this is a blemish. One must attach the etrog to the side of the lulav specifically at its lower end (the place where it is held), as the holy Ari wrote in Sefer HaKavanot: the place of attachment of the etrog to the lulav is at its end, at the place of holding from below — for so the crown (atarah) is at the end of the foundation (yesod), in kabbalistic terms.
takeaways: The lulav is always held in the right hand, the etrog in the left — during the blessing and during the hakafot alike
One should not hold a prayer book in the same hand as the lulav or etrog
The etrog should be attached at the lower end of the lulav (the holding place), according to the kabbalistic tradition

paragraphs: Hahaqqapot ballulab bekol yemot hachag yukal lehaqqip et hatteba shebbebet hakkeneset ap al pi sheen aleha seper tora, deen hannachat seper tora al hatteba meakkebet bidbar hahaqqapot ki haiqqar lepi hassod bazeh hu hatteba, mihu otam bene adam sheen holekim lebet hakkeneset mechamat ones umannichim kisse echad min habbayit umaqqipim oto en zeh kelum deen zeh nechshab "teba", veim kol zeh nireh li- mi shehu choleh vei epshar lo lehaqqip teba bebet hakkeneset yannicha kisse bebeto veyannicha alayv seper tana"k veyaqqip kede shello lebattel mitzvat hahaqqapa, vehashshem yitbarek berachamayv lo yimna tob laholekim betamim:

clarification.explanation: During the hakafot with the lulav throughout the days of the festival, one may circle the bimah in the synagogue even if no Torah scroll happens to be placed on it at that moment, since placing a Torah scroll on the bimah is not a condition that invalidates the hakafot — the essential element, according to the esoteric tradition, is the bimah itself. But people who cannot go to the synagogue due to unavoidable circumstance, and instead place a chair in their home and circle it — this accomplishes nothing, since a plain chair is not considered a 'bimah.' Nevertheless, the Ben Ish Chai adds: one who is sick and cannot reach the synagogue to circle a bimah should place a chair in his home and place upon it a book of Tanach (not an empty chair) and circle it, so as not to entirely nullify the mitzvah of the hakafah — and God, in His mercy, does not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
takeaways: One may circle the synagogue's bimah for hakafot even without a Torah scroll currently placed on it
A plain chair at home is not considered a 'bimah' for hakafot, unless a Tanach is placed on it — a solution for a sick person unable to reach the synagogue
